title: TB7-20462
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): She appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated September 25, 2017, rejecting her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) is a citizen of China. She appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated September 25, 2017, rejecting her claim for refugee protection.

The appeal is allowed. Pursuant to section 111(1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) refers the matter to the RPD for redetermination by a differently constituted panel. BACKGROUND Claim Background

The Appellant is a citizen of China who made a claim for refugee protection as a result of her participation in an underground Christian church in China. In August, 2015, one of the church members was arrested and the Appellant immediately went into hiding.
The Appellant subsequently came to Canada in March, 2016 and since that time she has continued to practice her faith at the XXXX XXXX Assembly and was baptized in that church in June, 2016.

The Appellant did not initiate her refugee claim upon her arrival in Canada. Rather, the Appellant indicated that she merely wanted to practice her religion and planned to return to China after learning that her church in China had resumed its activities. However, in February, 2017 her church was raided by the Public Security Bureau (PSB). Shortly thereafter, the PSB went to the Appellant's home searching for her. As a result, the Appellant initiated her refugee claim in March, 2017.

Further details of the Appellant's claim are set out in the RPD Record and in the materials submitted by the Appellant. Rather than recite them here, I shall refer to them as necessary throughout these reasons. RPD Decision

The RPD rejected the Appellant's claim on three grounds. First, it concluded that the Appellant lacked a credible subjective fear of persecution, as revealed by her failure to commence her claim for refugee protection until a year after her arrival in Canada.

Second, the RPD found that the Appellant's account of experiencing a medical condition known as neurasthenia was not credible. This finding was significant because it was the Appellant's medical condition that led her to begin to follow Christianity.

Finally, the RPD rejected the sur place element of the Appellant's claim, finding that her attendance at a Christian church in Canada was not "reflective of sincere religious devotion." This finding was based in large measure on the RPD's previous findings related to delay and misrepresentation related to her religious practice while still in China.

The Appellant has a statutory right of appeal to the RAD from a decision of the RPD on questions of law, fact or mixed law and fact.1 The standard of review on such questions is correctness, where there is no issue of credibility of oral evidence.2 In defining this standard of review, the Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica held that the legislative purpose of the RAD is to serve as a "safety net" that would catch all mistakes made by the RPD.3 This requires the RAD to carry out its own independent analysis of the RPD record to determine whether, as submitted by the Appellant, the RPD erred.4 The RAD as a true specialized appeal tribunal must come to its own conclusions based on a fresh review of the evidence.5 ISSUES

The Appellant argues that the RPD's determination lacked both analysis and logic, particularly with respect to the intertwined issues of delay and the sur place claim. As such, I will focus my analysis on these two issues. ANALYSIS Delay

I agree with the Appellant that the RPD erred in its assessment of the Appellant's delay in seeking refugee protection. There were two considerations in this case that were central to the issue of delay, and that were not considered by the RPD.

The first is that the Appellant maintained that she had not, to her knowledge, been personally targeted when she left China and arrived in Canada. In fact, the Appellant's testimony was that she intended to return to China once she learned that her Chinese church had resumed its activities.

Second, as pointed out by counsel for the Appellant, if the Appellant's intention was to fabricate a refugee claim, it would make little sense for her to have joined a church shortly after her arrival in Canada, but then to delay in making a claim for a year. In these particular circumstances, it was incumbent on the RPD to consider the Appellant's membership and extensive activities with her Canadian church in its analysis of the Appellant's delay in seeking refugee protection. Sur Place
I similarly conclude that the RPD erred in its analysis of the Appellant's sur place claim to refugee status.
In rejecting this element of the claim, the RPD member stated: "[f]urther, the panel finds that the sur place basis is precluded by the claimant's failure to claim."6

If this is a statement of principle, it is incorrect. If it is a finding of fact, it is unsustainable on the basis of my previous findings with respect to the issue of delay. Completely missing from this part of the RPD's reasons is an analysis of the Appellant's explanation for her delay - that she intended to return home once her Chinese church resumed its activities and only sought refugee protection when it was targeted by the PSB.

It is also notable that in dismissing the Appellant's Canadian church activity as being insincere, the RPD did not consider the Appellant's relatively extensive testimony on her relationship with the church or her religious knowledge. As the Appellant notes, the Federal Court has found that, in order to arrive at a decision as to the genuineness of a refugee claimant's current beliefs, the RPD must provide: i) some analysis of the evidence and ii) some justification for the decision that joining a church is only for the purpose of supporting a claim for refugee protection.7

In this case, the RPD provided neither, aside from a passing mention of its flawed findings on delay and an oblique reference to what I assume were its findings on the Appellant's medical condition. I find that this analysis provided an insufficient basis on which to conclude that the Appellant's religious activity in Canada was not reflective of sincere religious devotion.

Having found that the RPD erred in its analysis of the Appellant's claim, the RAD must next consider the appropriate remedy. In some recent decisions, the RAD has found that, notwithstanding any errors that the RPD may have committed, there is insufficient evidence to establish that practicing Christians in Liaoning Province face a well-founded fear of persecution in that province.8

In these decisions, the RAD has provided a detailed examination of the documentary evidence found in the Board's National Documentation Package for China and has observed a conspicuous lack of documentation of religious repression in Liaoning Province.

However, I note that, unlike the facts in those recent decisions, in this case the Appellant has testified that the PSB raided her church, have referred to it as an "evil cult," and have actively been searching for the Appellant. The RPD's questioning of the Appellant on this crucial element of her claim was cursory and, in its reasons, the RPD member makes no specific finding with respect to the credibility of the Appellant's claim that the PSB are searching for her.

As a result, we are left with the following: i) a series of RPD findings that I have found cannot be sustained on appeal; ii) an assertion by the Appellant that the PSB have raided her church and are looking for her; and iii) a body of documentary evidence confirming that religious repression is a serious problem in China, but is silent on the particular situation in Liaoning Province.

In these circumstances, the RAD is left with no option but to return this matter to the RPD for redetermination. Because of my conclusions with respect to the RPD decision, I cannot find that the presumption of truthfulness in respect of the Appellant's testimony has been rebutted. On the particular facts before me, I do not conclude that the absence of documentation of religious repression in Liaoning Province is sufficient, on its own, to rebut that presumption.

However, because the RPD's questioning of the Appellant on the issue of the PSB activities was minimal, and because the documentary evidence raises concerns as to the credibility of the claim that the PSB are searching for her, this matter must be heard afresh by the Refugee Protection Division.

The appeal is allowed. Pursuant to section 111(1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD refers the matter to the RPD for redetermination by a differently constituted panel.
